problem: Session 119's lab produced two YAML files — a Deployment and a Service — for one application. A realistic version of the ethics-triage stack has closer to six or eight: Deployments and Services for ethics- api and ethics-triage, a StatefulSet and PersistentVolumeClaim for ethics-db, a ConfigMap for non-secret configuration, NetworkPolicies from Session 117's cluster-wide hardening, and an Ingress. Multiply that by dev, staging, and production environments — each needing slightly different replica counts, resource limits, and image tags — and plain YAML stops scaling. You end up hand-editing near-duplicate files, or writing brittle sed commands like the one from Session 119's automation section, just to change a single value per environment.

Helm exists to solve exactly this: package a whole application's worth of Kubernetes manifests as one versioned, configurable unit, so 'deploy the ethics stack to staging with 2 replicas' is one command instead of editing eight files by hand.
concept: Helm is the de facto package manager for Kubernetes. A Helm chart is a directory of templated YAML manifests plus a single values file of configuration — install a chart, and Helm renders the templates with those values and applies the result to the cluster as one tracked unit called a release.

Term What it is Chart A packaged collection of templated Kubernetes manifests Values The configuration (replica count, image tag, resource limits) fed into a chart's templates Release A specific, named deployment of a chart with a specific set of values, tracked by Helm Repository A place charts are published and versioned (like a registry, but for charts) The relationship to Session 119 is direct: a chart is just the Deployment/Service/StatefulSet manifests from that session, with the parts that vary (image tag, replica count, resource limits) replaced by template placeholders filled in from values.
deep: Chart anatomy ethics-stack/ Chart.yaml # name, version, description values.yaml # default configuration templates/ api-deployment.yaml api-service.yaml db-statefulset.yaml configmap.yaml charts/ # any dependency sub-charts Templating — Go templates over YAML Helm templates are plain YAML with Go template syntax dropped in wherever a value needs to vary.
This is the direct fix for Session 119's sed-based tag substitution — instead of text-replacing a raw manifest, the manifest declares a placeholder and Helm fills it in properly.
# templates/api-deployment.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata:

image: registry/ethics-api tag: "1.4.2" # Session 118's immutable tag discipline, now parameterized replicas: 3 memoryLimit: 256Mi Environment-specific overrides A separate, small values-staging.yaml overrides only what differs from the default, keeping environment differences explicit and minimal rather than duplicating entire manifest files:

replicas: 1 memoryLimit: 128Mi helm install ethics-staging ./ethics-stack -f values-staging.yaml helm install ethics-prod ./ethics-stack -f values-prod.yaml Releases — Helm's tracked, versioned installs Every helm install or helm upgrade creates a new tracked revision of a release, stored in the cluster itself. This gives Helm a genuine rollback command, not just 'reapply an old file and hope':
helm upgrade ethics-prod ./ethics-stack -f values-prod.yaml # deploy v1.5.0 helm rollback ethics-prod 1 # instantly back to the previous release revision
workflow: Applied as the natural packaging step for the ethics stack once Session 119's raw manifests exist for dev, staging, and production:

1. Convert the working Deployment, Service, and StatefulSet YAML from Session 119's lab into templates under templates/, replacing hardcoded values (image tag, replica count, resource limits) with {{ .Values.* }} placeholders.
2. Define sensible defaults in values.yaml — these become the baseline every environment starts from.
3. Create a small values-<env>.yaml per environment containing only the overrides that genuinely differ (replica count, resource limits, maybe a different domain for Ingress).

4. Package and validate locally before ever touching a cluster: helm template ./ethics-stack -f values- staging.yaml — this renders the final YAML without applying it, letting you review exactly what would be deployed.
5. Install into staging: helm install ethics-staging ./ethics-stack -f values-staging.yaml.

6. For a code change, bump the tag in values-prod.yaml (still following Session 118's immutable-tag discipline) and run helm upgrade — Helm handles the rolling update via the same Kubernetes Deployment mechanics from Session 119.
7. If anything goes wrong, helm rollback ethics-prod <previous-revision> is immediate — no need to reconstruct what the old manifests looked like.
enterprise: Helm sits between raw Kubernetes manifests and the application teams who need to deploy repeatedly across multiple environments — it's the layer that makes 'deploy this app to a new environment' a one- command, low-error-surface operation instead of a manual YAML-editing exercise.

Layer Role Kubernetes cluster Runs whatever manifests are applied to it — unaware Helm exists Layer Role Helm chart Templated, versioned packaging of an application's full manifest set Chart repository Central, versioned store of charts — internal ones for CEx-built tooling, public ones for common services (databases, monitoring agents) you don't want to hand-write manifests for CI/CD pipeline Runs helm upgrade as the deploy step, parameterized per environment A large share of 'install this open-source tool into your cluster' instructions in the wild are, in practice, a single helm install command against a public chart — Helm's value isn't only for your own applications, it's also the standard way third-party infrastructure tools get installed.
dependencies: A working Kubernetes cluster and valid manifests (Session 119) — Helm has nothing to template if the underlying YAML structure isn't already correct.
The Helm CLI, which talks to the cluster using the same credentials/context kubectl uses.

A chart repository (Artifact Hub for public charts, or a private OCI registry / chart museum for internal ones) if charts are to be shared or versioned centrally rather than used only from a local directory.
Go template syntax knowledge for anything beyond simple value substitution — conditionals and loops in templates use the same {{ }} syntax with added logic.
dependents: GitOps tools (ArgoCD, Flux) frequently deploy Helm charts directly, watching a Git repository of chart+values and reconciling the cluster to match automatically.

Most public infrastructure components you'd add to a cluster (ingress controllers, monitoring stacks, cert-manager) are distributed and installed as Helm charts, so any cluster work beyond your own application eventually touches Helm.
Multi-environment CI/CD pipelines lean on Helm's per-environment values files to deploy the same versioned chart consistently across dev/staging/production.
Rollback and release-auditing processes depend on Helm's revision history as the record of exactly what was deployed and when.
security: Risk Mitigation Secrets committed directly into a values.yaml file Never put real credentials in values files tracked in Git;

use a Secrets manager or Helm Secrets/SOPS integration instead Installing untrusted public charts blindly helm template first to review rendered output before ever helm install-ing an unfamiliar chart Chart templates silently drifting from Session 117's hardening baseline Bake non-root/capability/resource-limit defaults into the chart templates themselves, not left to every values file to remember No visibility into what changed between releases helm diff (plugin) or reviewing rendered output before every upgrade, especially in production Overly broad RBAC granted to Helm's service account in-cluster Scope Helm's permissions to only the namespaces it needs to manage, per Session 119's RBAC guidance A habit worth building early Run `helm template` before every install or upgrade against production. It costs nothing and shows you exactly what YAML is about to be applied — the same discipline as reviewing a diff before merging code.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause First Command helm install fails with a templating error Invalid Go template syntax or a missing values key helm template ./chart -f values.yaml (renders without applying) Release stuck in 'pending-upgrade' A prior upgrade was interrupted mid- way helm status <release>; helm rollback if needed Rendered manifest doesn't match what you expected A values override wasn't applied, or file order was wrong helm template with -f files in the same order used for install "cannot re-use a name that is still in use" A release with that name already exists in the namespace helm list -A; use a different release name or upgrade instead Rollback doesn't fully restore old behavior Some resources (like PersistentVolumeClaims) aren't rolled back by Helm by design Check Helm's documented rollback scope for stateful resources
example: A realistic pattern once the ethics stack is running in Kubernetes: a single ethics-stack chart with three values files (dev, staging, prod), deployed via CI/CD with the release name and values file selected by which branch or environment triggered the pipeline. A bug fix ships as: bump the image tag in Chart.yaml's app version and values-prod.yaml, helm upgrade, and if the new version's health checks fail, one helm rollback command restores the previous known-good release without anyone needing to remember what the old manifests looked like.

Pattern to notice The chart itself rarely changes day to day — it's the stable, reviewed structure. Only the values file changes on a typical deploy, which is exactly what keeps routine deployments low-risk.
cloud: Every managed Kubernetes offering treats Helm as a first-class, expected tool rather than something separate to set up:

Platform Helm integration Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Google's own Marketplace deploys many solutions as Helm charts under the hood AWS EKS AWS documentation and EKS Blueprints lean heavily on Helm for add-ons Azure AKS Charts are the standard install path for AKS extensions and popular add-ons Cloud-managed Kubernetes doesn't change anything about how Helm itself works — the charts and values files are fully portable between a local minikube cluster (Session 119's lab) and a production GKE cluster, which is precisely the point of packaging deployments this way.
automation: Helm slots directly into the CI/CD deploy step from Session 119, replacing the fragile sed-based tag substitution with a proper, typed values override:

# CI/CD deploy step, replacing Session 119's sed approach - name: Deploy via Helm run: | helm upgrade --install ethics-prod ./ethics-stack \ -f values-prod.yaml \ --set api.tag=${{ github.sha }} \ --wait --timeout 5m - name: Verify rollout run: helm status ethics-prod --install makes this idempotent (creates the release if it doesn't exist, upgrades it if it does — safe to run on every deploy), and --wait blocks the pipeline until Kubernetes reports the rollout genuinely healthy, catching a failed deploy before the pipeline reports success.
career: Helm literacy is assumed, not optional, for most Kubernetes-adjacent roles — job postings that list Kubernetes experience very often expect Helm in the same sentence, since almost no real-world cluster is managed purely with raw kubectl apply.

It's also a strong, concrete artifact for your portfolio: packaging the CEx tooling stack as a chart with dev/staging/prod values files is the kind of thing you can show and walk through in an interview, demonstrating the full arc from Session 114's single Dockerfile to a templated, multi-environment, rollback-capable deployment.

misconceptions: Misconception Reality Helm is a replacement for Kubernetes manifests It generates the same manifests via templating — nothing about the underlying objects changes A chart's default values.yaml is meant for production Defaults are a baseline; production should always layer explicit overrides helm rollback restores everything perfectly Some resources, notably persistent data, are outside Helm's rollback scope by design Public charts are always safe to install as-is Review rendered output first — a chart can request broad RBAC permissions or run privileged containers Misconception Reality You need Helm even for a single simple app For one Deployment and Service in one environment, plain manifests are often simpler and sufficient
anchors: Chart = recipe. Values = the specific ingredients for tonight's dinner. Release = the actual meal you served, tracked so you can remake or undo it.
helm template = 'show me the manifest before I commit to anything' — the dry run that costs nothing.
Environment differences should live in a small overrides file, not in three near-duplicate copies of the whole chart.
helm upgrade --install is the idempotent habit — safe to run whether the release exists yet or not.

lab: Hands-on: convert Session 119's raw ethics-api manifests into a Helm chart with dev and prod values, and exercise a real upgrade/rollback cycle.

15. Scaffold a chart: helm create ethics-stack, then delete the generated example templates and replace them with your own api-deployment.yaml and api-service.yaml from Session 119, adding {{ .Values.* }} placeholders for image tag, replicas, and memory limit.
16. Fill in sane defaults in values.yaml (e.g. replicas: 1, tag: "1.0").
17. Create values-prod.yaml with replicas: 3 and a higher memory limit.
18. Render and review before installing anything: helm template ./ethics-stack -f values-prod.yaml | less — confirm the values were substituted correctly.
19. Install into your Session 119 minikube cluster: helm install ethics-prod ./ethics-stack -f values- prod.yaml, and confirm 3 replicas come up.
20. Simulate a release: bump tag in values-prod.yaml to a different (even fake) value and run helm upgrade ethics-prod ./ethics-stack -f values-prod.yaml --wait.
21. Check revision history: helm history ethics-prod, then roll back: helm rollback ethics-prod 1 and confirm the original tag is running again via kubectl get pods -o yaml | grep image.

Production tie-in Step 7's rollback is the exact recovery path you'd reach for if a real CEx tooling deploy shipped a regression — no manual YAML reconstruction, one command back to the last known-good release.
